subject: Computer Networking
title: IP: The Internet's Addressing System
description: A 60-second lesson on IP: The Internet's Addressing System.

hook.text: Every packet on the internet carries two addresses: where it's from and where it's going. That's IP.

buildup.text: IP stands for Internet Protocol. It handles addressing and routing — nothing more.

discovery.text: IP doesn't guarantee delivery or order. It just labels each packet and sends it toward the destination.

twist.text: Higher protocols like TCP add reliability on top. IP stays simple on purpose — complexity belongs elsewhere.

climax.text: Every device, phone, server, and smart fridge needs an IP address to participate on the internet.

punchline.text: IP puts an address on every packet. That's its only job.

details.summary: IP assigns a unique numerical address to every device on a network, enabling routers to forward packets to the correct destination across the internet. IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses while IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses to solve the exhaustion of the four-billion IPv4 address space.
details.whyItMatters: IP addressing is the foundation of all internet communication. Every packet of data you send or receive is routed based on IP addresses, making this the most fundamental networking concept.
takeaways: IPv4 addresses use 32 bits, providing about 4.3 billion addresses
IPv6 expands to 128 bits for virtually unlimited addresses
Routers use IP addresses to forward packets hop by hop

faq.question: Why is IPv4 running out of addresses?
faq.answer: IPv4 provides about 4.3 billion addresses, which seemed sufficient when designed in 1981. The explosion of smartphones, IoT devices, and cloud services exhausted the pool. NAT extended IPv4's life by sharing one public address among many devices, but IPv6 is the long-term solution.

faq.question: What does an IPv6 address look like?
faq.answer: IPv6 addresses are written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons, like 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334. Leading zeros in each group can be omitted, and consecutive groups of zeros can be replaced with a double colon for brevity.
